title: Indian Travelers Can Now Pay With UPI in Uzbekistan After Modi Visit Deal
excerpt: Uzbekistan becomes the 11th country to accept India'\''s digital payment system, letting tourists, students and business visitors pay merchants directly from Indian bank accounts.
body:
• NPCI International and Uzbekistan's NIPC signed a commercial agreement on August 30 to enable UPI-based merchant payments across the country via UZQR codes.
  • Uzbekistan becomes the 11th country to accept UPI, joining Singapore, the UAE, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Bhutan, Qatar, Sri Lanka, Cambodia and Greece.
  • Indian tourists, business travelers and students can pay directly from Indian bank accounts, avoiding foreign exchange markup on international cards.
  • The deal was signed during Prime Minister Modi's bilateral visit to Tashkent, with approvals from the RBI and the Central Bank of Uzbekistan.

Indian travelers heading to Uzbekistan will soon be able to leave their international cards at home. A new agreement signed during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Tashkent makes Uzbekistan the 11th country to accept India's Unified Payments Interface, extending the reach of the world's largest real-time payment system deeper into Central Asia.

NPCI International Payments Ltd. (NIPL), the overseas arm of the National Payments Corporation of India, signed the commercial agreement with Uzbekistan's National Interbank Processing Centre JSC (NIPC) on August 30, 2026. NIPC operates HUMO, Uzbekistan's national payment system.

How It Works

Under the agreement, Indian travelers can scan Uzbekistan's national interoperable QR code — called UZQR — using their existing UPI-enabled apps to make instant person-to-merchant payments. Money is debited directly from the user's Indian bank account, eliminating the need for cash exchange or international card transactions.

Because the Central Bank of Uzbekistan mandates HUMO's QR network across retail, hospitality and service outlets, UPI is expected to achieve near-universal merchant acceptance once the rollout is complete. No specific launch date has been announced yet, according to MediaNama.

"The initiative advances digital public infrastructure cooperation and aligns with both nations' broader strategic and economic goals."

— India's Ministry of Finance

UPI's Growing International Footprint

Uzbekistan joins a list of 10 countries that already accept UPI payments: Singapore, the United Arab Emirates, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Bhutan, Qatar, Sri Lanka, Cambodia and Greece. Each integration follows a similar pattern — bilateral agreements between NIPL and local payment operators, backed by regulatory approvals from both central banks.

The expansion is part of India's broader push to internationalise its digital public infrastructure. The Reserve Bank of India has been actively promoting cross-border payment linkages, including ongoing discussions within the BRICS framework on connecting fast payment systems and central bank digital currencies.

MEA Secretary (West) Sibi George confirmed the development during a press briefing, calling it another step in "the global expansion of Indian digital infrastructure."

Why Uzbekistan Matters

Uzbekistan may not be the most obvious destination for Indian travelers, but the Silk Road nation has been gaining traction. Home to UNESCO World Heritage sites in Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva, the country offers blue-tiled mosques, sprawling bazaars and mountain escapes that are drawing a growing number of Indian tourists.

For business travelers and the small but growing population of Indian students in Uzbekistan, the ability to pay in rupees directly — without currency conversion fees or international card markups — removes a practical friction point.

HUMO's Cross-Border Ambitions

The Uzbek side is no stranger to cross-border payment partnerships. HUMO is already connected to Ant International's Alipay+ network, with pilot integrations for AlipayHK and TNG eWallet. The system links 35 local banks and 42 non-bank financial institutions in Uzbekistan, giving it broad domestic coverage.

For India, the agreement fits a pattern of using bilateral payment linkages to deepen economic ties, reduce transaction costs for citizens abroad and position UPI as a credible alternative to the card networks that dominate international payments. With each new country added, the case for UPI as global infrastructure grows a little stronger.
